utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. All the accused are here. I think Defence teams are also a full house. Yes. And Mr. McCloskey is appearing for the Prosecution. I see Mr. McCloskey on his feet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. Mr. Lazarevic had identified another small section relating to the indictment, and those two, where there was no evidence on. And would you like me to just acknowledge that orally, or we can file something as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can file something. I think it will be useful. Or else you make a passing reference to it on Monday, when you start your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can file something very simply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's, I think, your turn, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, the question today is whether the Prosecution has adduced evidence such as to warrant convicting General Miletic for the counts alleged in the indictment. We say, no, they did not bring this evidence. First of all, I shall review the evidence pertaining to crimes against humanity, deportation. Crimes against humanity, the Prosecutor did not bring all the constitutive elements of that crime. Then, concerning General Miletic in particular, the Prosecution did not bring any evidence -- sufficient evidence of his taking part in the joint criminal enterprise and of his intention to justify -- to justify his conviction should have been criminal. I am therefore pleading for the acquittal of General Miletic of all counts concerning him; in particular, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. First of all, I will look at count number 8, the crime against humanity of deportation. In paragraph 84 of the indictment, the Prosecution alleges deportations were perpetrated, the forced displacement of Muslim men from Zepa who had to cross the Drina River to Serbia. This displacement of population by restricting the aid and bombardments and attack, but the only thing which could distinguish this from the forced transfer in count number 7 is the crossing of the Drina River, passing the border. In the indictment, the only people who crossed the river were the Muslim men of Zepa. Therefore, the only victims of this deportation would have been Muslim men of Zepa. Following Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal, crimes against humanity must have been committed during an armed conflict, whether international or domestic, and directed against a civilian population, whatever is this population. In his report of the 8th May 1993, paragraph 47, the Secretary-General of the United Nations wrote that crimes against humanity are directed against a civilian population. Those are those specific crimes against civilian population. In the Blaskic case, the Appeals Chamber considered, on its judgement of the 29th of July, 2004, at paragraph 107, that both the status of victim as a civilian, as a scale on which it's committed, or the level or organisation involved characterize a crime against humanity; therefore, it is not enough that the attack itself be directed towards the civilian population, it is not enough that civilian zones be bombarded and attacked, shelled. Victims have to be civilians. Now, in this case, we are talking about deportation. Therefore, it would have been necessary that the victims of deportation, those who crossed the River Drina, should have been civilians -- have to be civilians. Now, in the case at hand, we know that the individuals who were allegedly deported were men and able-bodied men of military age. Nobody may reasonably presume that these men were civilians, since a reasonable presumption would rather suggest that these men were considered as military. The fact of a victim being a civilian is one of the elements which constitutes the crime against humanity, and it is for the Prosecution to prove all the elements of the crime, including the status of individuals who fell victim to such action. Now, we have no evidence that these men were civilians. The Prosecution never deduced the slightest evidence that these men were not military. We have heard Witness PW-155, who crossed the Drina after the fall of Zepa. On the 5th of February, 2007, page 6831 of the transcript, this witness acknowledged and admitted that he was on the defence line, that he took part in the defence of Zepa, and this amounts to being a combatant. Then we heard Witness 49, who stated, on the 2nd of April, 2007, at page 9826, when talking about the brigade of Zepa, that part of these troops were armed and some of them succeeded in making it to Serbia. On 7th of November, 2007, at page 17633, speaking about military forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zepa, General Smith stated that these continued to fight in the area and that in most cases they crossed the Drina into Serbia. Therefore, those who crossed the Drina, who left for Serbia, were members of military forces, those who were fighters and were continuing to fight. Last, the military expert, Richard Butler, stated on the 17th of January, 2008, and this is at page 19945, that the members of the Army of the Republika Srpska were speaking about what they were actually seeing, i.e., Muslim soldiers who, rather than to surrender to the Army of Republika Srpska, were trying to cross the River Drina and to go to Serbia. Therefore, we know that an individual who took part in the defence of Zepa crossed the River Drina, that part of the armed troops belonging to the Zepa Brigade, the military forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, those who continued to fight and the Muslim soldiers. There can be no doubt about that. There are no civilians among those who passed the River Drina. The Prosecutor never adduced the slightest evidence that these men, who fled Zepa towards Serbia, were not military, while in order to prove a crime against humanity, he should have done so. Since the Prosecutor has not given any evidence that the men who crossed the River Drina were civilians, he failed to furnish the proof of the existence of the crime against humanity, which is deportation, and therefore General Miletic should be acquitted of that count. I will now speak about the alleged participation of General Miletic in a criminal -- joint criminal enterprise aimed at expulsing -- deporting the population from Zepa, Muslim population from Zepa. General Miletic is accused of having taken part in a joint criminal enterprise to deport the population -- Muslim population from Zepa. According to the Prosecution, this criminal -- joint criminal enterprise was aimed to force transfer and deportation of the Muslim population from this enclave for individual murders, such as assassination, murder against humanity, and murder, a violation of the laws and customs of war, and persecution. This crime would have been the aim of this joint enterprise. The Appeal Chamber Judge decided, in the Brdjanin case in its judgement on the 3rd April, 2007, paragraph 365, that in order to be sentenced for taking part in the first form of the joint criminal enterprise, the accused must have had the intention to commit this crime and the intention to take part in the joint plan with the goal -- the goal of which was to commit this crime. Liability founded on the participation of an accused in a joint criminal enterprise requires the participation of the accused himself. Further to the judgement made in the Brdjanin case, paragraph 424, this participation may take the form of assistance or helping or contribution to the implementation of the common goal, but the Appeal Chamber decided in the same judgement, at paragraph 427, that any sort of behaviour does not equate to contribution sufficiently important to make the accused criminally liable. If the Appeal Chamber observed that this contribution shouldn't be substantial, nevertheless it decided at paragraph 430 that it has to be significant so that the accused may be judged as guilty. The Prosecutor, therefore, had to adduce the evidence of a significant participation of General Miletic in the joint criminal enterprise and of his intention to commit the crime and to take part in the joint plan to commit the forced transfer and deportations. What would be the evidence of General Miletic's participation to the joint criminal enterprise? Only his position in the General Staff of the Republika Srpska in 1995. And yet this position remains more than fuzzy, woolly. The Prosecutor tells us in the indictment, in French, that General Miletic was the chief of staff per interim, which is probably one of the possible translations of "standing in for." Now, all the witnesses, without any exception, including the military expert of the Prosecutor, stated that General Milovanovic was the chief of staff during all the war including in 1995, including in July 1995. General Milovanovic himself stated, on the 29th of May, 2007 - this can be read at page 12146 - that he was the head of -- the chief of staff of the Republika Srpska all along the war of -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he repeated this on the 31st of May, 2007, at page 12303. The other officers of the Army of Republika Srpska confirmed that General Milovanovic was, in July 1995, the chief of staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska. For instance, Mirko Trivic, on the 22nd of May, 2007, page 11937; Bogdan Sladojevic on the 27th of August, 2007, page 14388; Nedeljko Trkulja on the 10th of September, 2007, page 15074. Miomir Sakic on the 13th of September 2007, page 15323; Petar Skrbic on the 17th of September, 2007, at 15507. The officers of UNPROFOR also stated that General Milovanovic was the chief of -- was the chief of the Army of Republika Srpska and General Smith, commanding the armed forces for Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995 stated the same on the 7th of November, 2007, at page 17619. And General Nikolai, who was chief of staff, UNPROFOR, confirmed this on the 29th of November, 2007, page 18448. Edward Joseph also stated this on the 22nd of August, 2007, page 14148. Finally, the military expert of the Prosecutor, Richard Butler, also stated this during the hearing on the 23rd of January, 2008, pages 2240 to 241, that General Milovanovic was the general chief of staff -- the main chief of staff in July 1995. General Milovanovic is indeed the chief of staff of the Republika Srpska Army in 1995. He performs the duties, the obligations, and tasks as chief of staff. We have seen the documents he signed during all this period between March and July 1995, and we may mention P2687, a document concerning the convoys of the 7th of April, 2007, and also Exhibit P2669A, an order signed by General Milovanovic on the 27th of May, 1995. The Prosecutor shows the documents designating General Miletic as representative of the chief of staff. There is no doubt that his name is and features on these documents and that his duties are described as being the representative of the chief of staff, only nobody really knows what this term really means and what exactly is exactly the functions and duties of the representative of the chaff, what are his powers and what is his authority. The fact is that when General Milovanovic was physically absent from the staff, and I have to underscore "physically" because his absence was only physical, some of his duties, which he couldn't perform by reason of his physical absence, were performed by other generals. In his capacity as chief of staff, General Milovanovic had contact with UNPROFOR. General Nikolai stated on the 29th of November, 2007, at page 18448 that his principal contact was General Milovanovic, and he added that when General Milovanovic was not present, he spoke to other generals. Only General Miletic does not feature among the generals with whom General Nikolai had contacts. General Milovanovic, in his capacity of the General Staff, was going in the field. He did indeed go to Zvornik in April and May 1995, which is shown by Exhibits P2891, 5D714, and we know that General Miletic, in 1995, did not only even once go to check the status of the units on the ground, in the field. Other officers went there. On the 31st of May, 2007, and this is to be seen at page 12309, General Milovanovic said that General Miletic would put in for him for daily activities, and he added that General Miletic never had the powers -- all the powers which he, General Milovanovic, held. And on the 28th of January, 2008, at page 20548, the military expert of the Prosecutor stated that he did not believe that General Miletic had the authority or the powers enabling him to perform the duties which had been those of General Milovanovic. Based on all the evidence which we have seen, on the base of all the documents which bear the name of General Miletic as the representative of the chief of staff, nobody could reasonably conclude that General Miletic had totally replaced General Milovanovic in his capacity of chief of staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska. At most, these documents and evidence presented lead to a conclusion that General Miletic did sign some documents, and I say "some documents," when, for a reason or another, General Milovanovic was prevented from signing them. Once again, none of these documents bear the famous letters "SR" which means that it was personally signed by the person named in the document. According to the explanation given by the expert witness Richard Butler on the 17th of January, 2008, at page 19871 of the transcript. And If we follow the indictment, we can read that for the Prosecution, General Miletic would have been the principal adviser of General Mladic. There, again, there is no evidence. Indeed, during his statement of the 21st of August, 2006, at page 383, the Prosecutor quoted the names of four generals, including General Miletic, who would have been the closest adviser or closest officer of General Mladic. The only thing is that this thesis is supported by no evidence. Differently from all other generals of the staff and differently from all the commanders of the corps, who were all subordinated directly to General Mladic, General Miletic was not even a direct subordinate. He was subordinated to General Milovanovic. General Milovanovic stated on the 31st of May, 2007, page 12303, as well as Richard Butler on the 28th of January, 2007, at page 20547, stated that because General Mladic was not a direct superior of General Miletic, General Miletic had no reason to have direct contacts or regular contacts with General Mladic. Besides, General Milovanovic affirmed on the 31st of May, 2007, at page 12311 that General Mladic did not particularly like General Miletic. We have heard, on the 5th and 6th of November, 2007, General Smith speak of a lot of meetings he had with General Mladic in 1995, and we saw minutes or reports of these meetings. Those are Exhibits P2933, P2934, P2942, P2943, P2747, P2947. We can only notice total absence of General Miletic at these meetings. No trace of his presence, no evidence that General Mladic would have consulted him before such meetings or even would have had transmitted the results of the meetings after those. No, nothing much. The Prosecutor will certainly say that General Miletic was not in charge of these meetings, in particular with UNPROFOR or with international organisations. Agreed. But in that case, how could he have had the central pivotal role in the distribution of humanitarian aid? I shall come back on this point later. For the moment, let us accept that his role was not to deal or prepare meetings, but to help General Mladic in military operations. During the Srebrenica operation in July 1995, General Mladic came in the field, on the ground, and we know that he is present on the 11th of July, 1995. General Mladic is at Srebrenica, but without General Miletic. Several meetings took place on the 11th and 12th of July in Bratunac. I shall not speak of the meetings in the Hotel Fontana, but I note that General Miletic is not present. What is most significant is that on the 11th or 12th of July, 1995, is that a meeting would have taken place in Bratunac, where the continuation of military actions towards Zepa was decided and planned, elaborated. Mirko Trivic stated on the 21st of May, 2007, at page 11841 to 842 that General Mladic was present at least for part of the meeting, for part of the meeting, but General Miletic did not -- was not present, did not attend. No proof -- no evidence exists that General Mladic consulted the general before this meeting or that he informed him of the conclusions or decisions made in this meeting, after it had taken place. Simply, there is no evidence that at the time, General Mladic would have contacted General Miletic or that General Mladic wanted to contact, not even that he tried to contact him. We also know that General Mladic went to Zepa. Many witnesses confirmed this point. General Smith, on the 6th of November, 2007, page 17556; Edward Joseph on the 23rd of August, 2007, page 14160; Thomas Dibb on the 15th of October, 2007, page 16293; Witness 49 on the 30th of March, 2007, page 9729 and 9732, and as well as reports such as P2946 and P2944. As for General Miletic, he did not go to Zepa in 1995, not even once before that, during or after the military actions which happened there. He did not help General Mladic either in Zepa nor in conducting military action, nor in the negotiations which he, himself, Mladic, had conducted on the spot. We also know that General Mladic took part in the departure of General Zivanovic on the 20th of July, 1995, in the Jela Restaurant, accompanied by his chief of staff, General Milovanovic. General Milovanovic confirmed this on the 29th of May, 2007, page 12206, as well as Mirko Trivic on the 21st of May, 2007, at page 11876. Once again, General Miletic was not present. We finally know that all the generals of the Main Staff were present at Banja Luka at the beginning of August 1995 to sign the letter which was supporting General Mladic, and this is Exhibit P1026. Once again, General Miletic was not present. Isn't this a strange adviser, who never accompanies the one he should be advising? Obviously, General Miletic is not accompanying General Mladic. This is not all. No element of the case file indicates that General Mladic ever contacted General Miletic to ask him some advice. Once again, there is absolutely nothing. In the indictment, the Prosecutor sustains that General Miletic was the main officer in charge of transcribing the intentions, orders, and directives of the commander. Agreed, but then one had to prove that he had done so for Srebrenica and Zepa, and this is not at all the case. Indeed, we have directive number 7, but directive number 7 is not even a directive from the commander. It is from the Supreme Command, President Karadzic. Let us examine this directive number 7, which is Exhibit P5, for its face value without entering a possible interpretation of what it means or what is the meaning of the sentence concerning civilian population in the enclaves. We do not deny that General Miletic had taken part in its drafting, the drafting of this directive, but he did not actually conceive it. He did not formulate it. This text is not his text. It is the text of the Supreme Command, President Karadzic. In his statement on the 21st of August, 2006, page 399, the Prosecutor stated that General Miletic, in person, had drafted the sentence concerning the civilian population in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, but during the presentation of evidence, he did not show in any way that General Miletic had written or drafted this sentence. He in fact carefully avoided this matter. Now, on the 30th of May, 2007, at page 11277, General Milovanovic stated that President Karadzic may have added this sentence against the will and wish of General Miletic and that, anyway, even if General Miletic had opposed this, this opposition would have led to nothing. On the 29th of January, 2008, pages 20585 to 586, the military expert of the Prosecution confirmed that Radovan Karadzic may have modified or amended certain parts of the directive before he signed it, and that he may have added this sentence against the will of the members of the staff. The question of knowing who wrote or drafted this sentence remains completely open. Was it General Mladic who after his meeting with General Smith on the 5th of March, 1995, where he announced there would be a restriction on the convoys General Smith spoke about it on the 6th of November, 2007, at page 17478, and indeed what General Mladic said was reported in an UNPROFOR report dated 6th March 1995, Exhibit P2933. Was it President Karadzic who added this sentence for some reason or another? We do not know. But the Prosecution gave us no evidence, and also he furnished no evidence that General Miletic would have written it or drafted it. Now, the onus probandi is for the Prosecutor. He should have furnished his evidence for his argument according to which General Miletic would have written this sentence, and he has not done so. The fact that the name General Miletic features on this directive is no evidence, because this directive was not his. It emanates from President Karadzic. At most, what can be concluded from this directive is the fact that General Miletic would have known about the general policy concerning the enclaves, knowledge, but not the fact that he would adhere to this policy. And further to this directive, we also have directive 7.1, Exhibit 361, a directive in which the sentence in question does not feature. If General Mladic wrote this sentence concerning the civilian population at Srebrenica and Zepa, he may have thought again and changed his mind, if it was President Karadzic who had written it. General Mladic may probably have decided not to follow these directives. Whatever the case may be, on the basis of the evidence presented in this case file, this sentence cannot be put at the door of General Miletic. The Prosecutor wants us to believe that directive 7 and 7.1 were the starting point -- the cause of the future events which took place in Srebrenica and Zepa, and besides the date of directive number 7 on the 8th of March, 1995, is the date of the creation of the joint criminal enterprise which is alleged. The Prosecutor did not bring any evidence that those directives had as an aim to attack Srebrenica or Zepa. He adduced no evidence of a nexus of causality between this directive and the elements which took place in the eastern enclaves of Bosnia, in the enclaves of eastern Bosnia in 1995. The orders of General Milovanovic initiating military action around Srebrenica, which referred to the directives, do not countenance the taking of the enclaves. The taking of the enclaves was a sudden decision made on the 9th of July, in the evening, and I will express myself on this a bit later. None of these two directives, 7 and 7.1, mentions an attack against the enclaves. Directive 7.1 does not even speak of the enclaves. The directive just speaks about the separation of the enclaves. And since this directive indicates that the enclaves have to be separated, obviously it does not envisage to deport the Muslim population, because without the Muslim population, the enclaves would not have existed, and therefore separating them would have had no reason. The separation of the enclaves, which is envisaged in the directive, did not envisage the transfer of population. This is not a crime. This is a military objective, an objective which was actually consistent and consonant with the agreement signed in 1993 between the Army of the Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and UNPROFOR. The Prosecutor needs directive 7 for -- in this case. He thinks that this directive, mentioning humanitarian convoys, may tie up General Miletic to the events which took place in July 1995 at Srebrenica and Zepa, but do we have evidence that the restriction to humanitarian aid increased after the directive? A great number of orders concerning the passage of convoys show that this policy, this controlled policy, already existed since the beginning of the war. Besides, do we have any evidence that humanitarian aid was particularly restricted in the case of Srebrenica and Zepa? No, we do not have any. The policy towards convoys was the same for all the enclaves. Do we have any evidence that the humanitarian situation in the enclaves was a consequence of the restrictions imposed on the convoys? No, we don't have any. We know or saw that there were some foul play taking place. Exhibits 5D31 and 5D509 affirm this. But whatever the case, the situation in Srebrenica, as such, could very well be a consequence of this foul play of the Bosnian authorities locally and for which General Miletic is not at all responsible. The Prosecutor brought evidence that the restriction to humanitarian aid was the cause of the humanitarian situation at Srebrenica, but he did not do so. We have about 50 reports of the Zvornik Brigade which show the number of convoys which went through to go to Srebrenica and Zepa during the period from March to July 1995, and we have the document of UNPROFOR, Exhibit 5D728, which states that in March, 93 per cent of the humanitarian aid provided for Srebrenica reached, indeed, Srebrenica. 93 per cent is practically the total. Yes, the name of General Miletic does appear on the documents, which are only information sent to the subordinated units to inform them that convoys may pass and to tell them what -- where the convoys for whom the passage was not allowed or authorised. Yes, his name does feature on this document, he was the chief of the administration in charge of operational matters, and he was therefore in charge of transmitting this type of information to the subordinated -- the units subordinated to the Main Staff. If one looks very carefully at these documents, one can see that for most of them, those were the United Nations UNPROFOR convoys, the passage of which were limited. Convoys of UNPROFOR did not transport humanitarian aid, and General Miletic is accused exclusively to have taken part in the restriction of humanitarian aid to the Muslim population. In his statement of the 21st of August, 2006, page 442, the Prosecutor declared that General Miletic played a very important role in the organisation of convoys and that he decided which were the convoys who could leave and those who couldn't. But he adduced no evidence that General Miletic decided anything concerning the convoys. The only element of evidence, just a shred of evidence which, by the way, does not confirm at all the argument of the Prosecutor, are two conversations, P1237 and P1266, which show that General Tolimir, together with General Mladic, were deciding about the passage. The Exhibit P1266 also shows that the coordinating organ gave the authorisations. We know that Colonel Djukic, an officer of the staff, was a member of this coordination unit. We have Exhibit 6D7, which lists the members of that organ. The military expert of the Prosecution, Richard Butler, confirmed on the 1st of February, 2008, on page 20950 that General Djordjic [realtime transcript read in error "Djukic"] was not subordinated to General Miletic. Besides, a great number of orders, Exhibit P2749, 5D372, 5D374, 5D378, 5D605, 5D725, signed by General Mladic, General Milovanovic, and even General Tolimir, which were given much before directive number 7, determined what were the lines concerning the procedures applied to the convoys. We have seen about meetings concerning humanitarian aid where General Miletic did not attend. We have seen orders concerning the passage of convoys signed by some generals, but none was signed by General Miletic. We have discovered that there was a unit or organ in charge of humanitarian aid presided by Professor Koljevic, whose role has not been elucidated. Finally, Exhibit 5D615 shows that the Ministry of Internal Affairs was also taking part in matters concerning the passage of convoys, and of course we do not know exactly what was the role of this Ministry. In all this, there is no evidence that General Miletic had any other role than to transmit information concerning the passage of convoys to the subordinated units. Beyond the fact that we have no evidence that General Miletic had personally signed these documents, the Prosecution himself, referring to -- in his statement of the 21st of August, 2006, at page 444, one of these documents which became later Exhibit P2497, stated that none of this was criminal, and indeed there is nothing criminal about these documents, nothing illegal or illicit. Humanitarian aid was partly used for the needs of the Muslim army. The convoys were a means of illegally bringing weapons in the enclaves, as is shown by Exhibits 5D518 and 5D519, and therefore certain restrictions were imposed and a control was performed. As the Prosecutor stated, this procedure does not contain any criminal elements. We can take it one step further. This procedure complies with the Geneva Conventions, Article 23, paragraph one of the 4th Geneva Convention provides as follows: "Each high contracting party shall allow the free passage of all consignments of medical and hospital stores and objects necessary for religious worship intended only for civilians of another high contracting party, even if the latter is its adversary. It shall likewise permit the free passage of all consignments of essential food stuffs, clothing and tonics intended for children under 15, expected mothers, and maternity cases." Furthermore, paragraph 2 of Article 23 of the Geneva Convention stipulates: "The obligation of a high contracting party to allow the free passage of the consignments indicated in the preceding paragraph is subject to the condition that this party is satisfied that there are no serious reasons for fearing, (a), that the consignments may be diverted from their destination; (b), that the control may not be effective, or, (c), that a definitive advantage may accrue to the military efforts or economy of the enemy." Indeed, when a warring party may have serious grounds for thinking that the scope and frequency of the consignment can foster the military efforts or the economy of the adversary, or if it has reasons to believe that the humanitarian aid is used for military purposes, it is entitled to deny the free passage. We have the judicial notice in this case that part of the humanitarian aid was used for the needs of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Even if we admit that for the sake of the argument, the passage of the consignments was restricted and that the situation, from a humanitarian standpoint in the enclaves, was bad, nonetheless the Prosecutor has not demonstrated that the policy that applied to the convoys was a consequence of directive number 7, and the consequence was due to the restriction imposed on the convoys. The Prosecution did not demonstrate what the part -- what part was played by General Miletic in the implementation of such a policy, other than he sent information to his subordinates. Other than that, the Prosecution did not demonstrate that the procedure that applied to the convoys, which was fully compliant with the Geneva Convention, was aimed at driving out the Muslim population from the enclaves. I shall now address the situation on the ground. What knowledge did General Miletic have of the situation on the ground, not only during the period when these events took place, but also before that, the events in Srebrenica and Zepa? In his opening statement on the 21st of August, 2007, the Prosecution stated the chief of operations is someone that is involved in the military operations of the corps and the brigade. This is not someone who is in charge of logistics. This is not someone who is in charge of technical matters. This is someone who truly operates on the ground. I shall not address this issue as to whether the Prosecutor attributed the right role to the person in charge of operations and whether this was his true role. I shall just say that at the time, the war was waged on all fronts in the Republika Srpska, in the areas of the 6th Corps and by a hundred or so brigades and other units. And the Prosecutor admits in its opening statement on the 21st of August, 2006, page 396, that in July 1995, the Sarajevo front line was a main front line for Serbs. Indeed, this is not Western Bosnia [as interpreted], but the Sarajevo front line and the Bihac front line, that concerned the Main Staff at the time. Line 23, we should read not "Western Bosnia" but "the Sarajevo front line and the Bihac front line." One should read "Eastern Bosnia" and not "Western Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever the case may be, it was simply impossible for the chiefs of operations of the Main Staff to operate on the ground and to take part in any military operation led by all the corps and brigades. Besides, the military expert of the Prosecutor contradicts this theory, for he restricts intervention of the Main Staff in military operations to very specific cases. He stated at the hearing of January 29, 2008, page 20587, and I quote: "It is only when several corps commanders needed to intervene that the issues were complex and that the relationships between the various commanders needed to be addressed, and that it was only then that the Main Staff intervened." But let's address the Prosecutor's case and see whether there is any evidence to show that the chief of operations did take part in some of these military operations. This is what we are interested in, but the answer is quite a simple one. There was none. During the presentation of its case, the Prosecutor provided no evidence to show that in 1995, General Miletic was on the ground in Western Bosnia during -- before, during and after the operations in Srebrenica and Zepa, and General Milovanovic ascertained, on the 31st of May, 2007, page 12311, that General Miletic was assigned on the front line for the last time when he was lieutenant colonel, so we are very far now from 1995. We know that some Main Staff officer did go to the area of the Drina Corps in the period running from March to July 1995, and amongst others General Milovanovic, the person who should have been in Western [as interpreted] Bosnia. General Milovanovic goes in April and then again in May 1995. Exhibits P2891 and 5D714 confirm that. General Milovanovic went there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you may want to clear up. I think there's been some translation issues that probably should be cleared up now. I hate to interrupt you, but I think you meant "1993" when you said -- it says "we are far from 1995."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say it, we are very far from 1995. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, and I think we've got "Western" and "Eastern" mixed up too, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have in the transcripts now, that there is no evidence from the Prosecution that General Miletic, in 1995, was ever on the ground in Western Bosnia, before, during, or after the operations in Srebrenica and Zepa; lines 20, 21 and 22 of page 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 18 should be read as "Eastern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Having said that, I think we can proceed, and then we can change whatever needs to be changed. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Therefore, General Milovanovic went to Eastern Bosnia in 1995, but General Miletic did not go there. We have no evidence that General Miletic went there before the Srebrenica operation to observe the state of the Muslim forces or the units of the Army of Republika Srpska. Besides, the observation of Muslim forces was not part of his assignment. This was the role of the intelligence services, and if these services in some armies belong to the same one -- the same department as the operations, as is the case in the British Army, where General Smith was in charge of the operations as well as security matters, as he stated on the 5th of November, 2007, pages 17462, 17463, this is not the case in the Army of the Republika Srpska, where, at the Main Staff level, these two departments are totally separate. Richard Butler confirmed this on the 28th of January, 2008, page 20581, that intelligence services and security matters are a separate branch under the responsibility of General Tolimir. But whatever the case may be, contrary to the other officers of the Main Staff, namely, General Milovanovic, who went several times during this period to the area under the responsibility of the Drina Corps, General Miletic in 1995 did not go there. Consequently, as far as the situation in the area of Srebrenica and Zepa is concerned, he can't have seen anything whatsoever. During this period, the Prosecutor mentioned several incidents. The Bratunac Brigade purportedly shelled Srebrenica on the 25th of May, 1995, following an order from the Main Staff. We do not dispute the shelling of the 25th of May, 1995, only we have never seen an order given by the Main Staff to that effect, and the Prosecutor provided no evidence of this order or that the order existed. We have no order from the Main Staff concerning this bombing, and we have no report informing the Main Staff that the shelling actually took place. We have no evidence to show that any information relating to this shelling ever reached the Main Staff. And once again General Miletic is not on the ground and can have no knowledge of these events, if the latter were not reported to the Main Staff. Then there was the takeover of the observation post by UNPROFOR, the Post Echo. Once again, we have no detailed information that could establish a connection between this and General Miletic. The Prosecutor would like us to believe that this action is a direct consequence of the order given by General Milovanovic on the 27th of May, 1995, but this is not the case. The two exhibits referred to by the Prosecutor on the 1st of February, 2008, at the testimony -- additional testimony of Mr. Butler, Exhibit P3161, and the Zvornik Brigade Exhibit P3162, only concerns UNPROFOR members who were deployed in Gorazde. Neither of these exhibits have any connection whatsoever with the Post Echo. However, P2894, which is the order of General Zivanovic, which relates to the operation that led to the takeover of the Post Echo, does not refer to any order or action on the part of the Main Staff. However, if we were to accept the theory of the Prosecution; i.e., that the events that took place at the Post Echo have anything to do with General Milovanovic, this theory is not inculpatory for General Miletic. Quite the contrary, it is exculpatory, because he is not solely in charge of Western Bosnia, he is there to give orders to the Drina Corps. General Miletic does not personify the Main Staff. He cannot be held responsible for the acts or conducts of other members of the Main Staff or other members of the army, and especially he cannot bear the responsibility for the orders of his superiors, which he did not carry out and which he probably was not even aware of. And we have no evidence that General Miletic purportedly took part, in one way or another, in the drafting of the order provided by General Milovanovic or that he would have had a hand in its implementation. The Srebrenica operation had been planned within the Drina Corps, and all the preparation work had been done by the Drina Corps. No document, no testimony, involves the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska; namely, the planning and preparation of this operation. Quite the contrary, Mirko Trivic confirmed on the 22nd of May, 2007, page 11194, that this was an operation led by the Drina Corps. The military expert of the Prosecution, Richard Butler, on the 29th of January, 2008, stated on page 20587, and I quote: "As far as Krivaja-95 is concerned and the entire planning process that it involves, this could really have been carried out by the corps or the corps chief of staff. It was, therefore, not necessary for the Main Staff to plan every detail of this operation." True to fact, on that same day, the 29th of January, 2008, page 20588, Richard Butler ascertained that it was not before the evening of the 9th of July that the Main Staff intervened in the Srebrenica operation. A lot of things happened in the course of that evening of the 9th of July, 1995. President Karadzic orders the operation to continue and to enter Srebrenica. This order given by President Karadzic profoundly changes the meaning of the Srebrenica operation. Richard Butler, the military expert, confirmed this on the 29th of January, 2008, page 20588, that the primary objective was the separation of the enclaves, and that the objective was changed during that evening on the 9th of July, 1995. This order, given by President Karadzic, was passed on by General Krstic to General Tolimir. This is Exhibit number P89 [as interpreted]. The document forwarding the order of President Karadzic is a document which, normally speaking, should have been written and signed by the officers who were part of the Operations Department. The military expert, on the 29th of January, 2008, stated at page 20590 that this document, P849, is exactly the type of document that the operations body would prepare, but this particular document, P849, the key document involving the Main Staff in the Srebrenica operation, did not leave the Operations Administration. It is not General Miletic who drafted it. It is not General Miletic who signed it. It is not General Miletic who sent it off. There is no evidence, either, that General Miletic had any knowledge of the fact at the time. Nobody explained why General Miletic and the administration in charge of military operations were not involved in the forwarding of this document to the Drina Corps, so we can only speculate on the matter. Either General Miletic was simply not present at the Main Staff at that time, which does not tell us why another officer in his administration did not draft this document or for one reason or another General Miletic and his administration were excluded from this part of the operation. Let me emphasise once again that logically, according to the military organisational structure of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Miletic should have, to all intents and purposes, been involved in the drafting of this document. Once again, I would like to stress this. The document is self-explanatory. General Miletic was not involved. This document proves, as clearly as not, that one cannot rely on someone's position to ascertain his responsibility. Material evidence need to be shown to -- that go to the acts and the conduct of a particular person. In the course of this trial, the Prosecutor insists on the duties of General Miletic, not his acts, and hoping thus that the Chamber would be convinced that his position was such that nobody could do without General Miletic within the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The Prosecution is so convinced of the importance of the position held up by General Miletic that it forgot to show the proof of his acts, the only proof that would sustain a conviction of General Miletic. This document, however, proves -- disproves the theory of the Prosecution. Indeed, the name of General Miletic is mentioned in the reports that pertain to the situation on the ground, but once again none of these reports mention "SR," which according to the report means "on behalf of" or should be signed by him personally. We know that during at that time, General Nikolai tried to contact someone, a general, never mind which one at the Main Staff, and we know that this happened on the 8th and 10th of July and that the reply came back saying that there was no one authorised to talk to him. Perhaps -- P2750 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2790"], P976 [as interpreted]. Perhaps General Miletic was not authorised to speak to the head of the Main Staff or UNPROFOR, or perhaps he just simply was not at the Main Staff. There are, at any rate, only these two possibilities; there isn't a third. These reports that bear the name of General Miletic and that were sent to President Karadzic, are the reports which were sent on a daily basis. These reports have no link whatsoever with Srebrenica. These reports were sent every day at the same time, whatever happened, no matter whether there was fighting or not. Since the beginning of the war, since the first day the Republika Srpska was formed, every day an officer in charge of the administration of military operations summarises and collates the information which is sent off to the 6th Corps and to the president of the corps -- of the Republic and to the corps. Following the order of President Karadzic, the order is completely unknown to General Miletic and his administration, and that is when the Army of the Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica. We then have the Main Staff document, that of General Mladic. None of these orders stem from General Miletic. We also have the order dated 11th of July, 1995, P3038, and then on the 13th of July, 1995, Exhibit 5DP35. Both bear the letters "SR." So two of these documents should have been signed by General Mladic personally. On the 11th and 13th of July, General Mladic was not at the Main Staff. General Miletic was there neither on the 11th and the 13th [as interpreted] . And General Mladic -- and there is no prove that General Miletic at the time had knowledge of these orders. Once again, the Prosecutor shows no evidence that General Miletic was purportedly involved, in one way or another, in the events in Srebrenica. All the knowledge that General Miletic may have had about the events in Srebrenica before and during the fighting, as well as after the Army of Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica, stem from the reports he received. These reports did not tell us much, and very often they were inaccurate. We are very far from the Prosecution's theory according to which General Miletic would have observed the status of the Muslim forces before, during, and after the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa, would have observed the surrender of the Muslim forces after the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa; would have observed the surrender, the activities of the VRS in the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa; would have followed up on the transfer of the civilian population from Zepa and Srebrenica. Besides, he was unable to observe or follow up on these activities for the simple reason that he wasn't there, neither he nor his subordinates were on the ground, besides other officers were present. How much does General Miletic know about the fall of Srebrenica and the transfer of the population? The only information that arrived was on the 12th of July, 1995. This reached the Main Staff and pertained to the transfer. This is contained in a report which was mentioned over the telephone from Potocari to Panorama. The code name is "Main Staff." This is recorded in the intercept of the 12th of July at 12.40. This is a short conversation, Exhibit number P1112, and the relevant part deserves to be read in its entirety. [In English]" We are starting the relocation of those who want to go toward Kladanj and entering force with trucks and buses, and a water tank should be sent to give them water and food. This morning, we organise it here. We will give them everything. I talked with them, and we will accept all of civilians who want to -- who want to and they can stay. Those who don't want to can choose where they will go." [Interpretation] Indeed, there is another intercept recorded ten minutes later that states the contrary, but this does not involve the Main Staff. The only information that reached the Main Staff and that General Miletic could therefore have had access to stated that everything had been organised, the water, the food, and those that wished to stay could stay, and those that wished to go could go and could choose where they wanted to go. A report indicates that the Geneva Conventions were fully respected, for if Article 49 of the 4th Geneva Convention prohibits forced transfer, paragraph 5 also prohibits forced retention. The involvement of General Miletic in the Srebrenica operation and the ensuing events are clearly stipulated in the conversation that was recorded on the 12th of July at 12.40, when two people, discussing the question of fuel, referred to a certain Miletic. The Miletic in question does not know where to find the fuel, and he does nothing to try and find it. The Prosecutor ascertains that the man in question is General Miletic. Well, so be it, in that case the Prosecution should accept that once again General Miletic has no knowledge of anything that he should have known about. And the impact of this conversation is even greater. General Miletic does nothing to try and find the fuel. He does not get involved. This is none of his business and he does not get involved. Of course, he is in charge of drafting the report, and he does. He drafts it on the basis of the reports he gets. He has no direct knowledge of what is happening on the ground. The Prosecutor will say that some documents were addressed to General Miletic, asking him for information or additional orders. Yes, there are some. We have Exhibit number P192, 13th of July, 1995, signed by Lieutenant Colonel Siromir Leftic [phoen], commander of the military police of the 65 Regiment of Protection, Zoran Malinic, should have contacted General Miletic, but we have no evidence that Zoran Malinic did anything, according to the document. Whatever the case may be, we do not even know whether General Miletic had occasion to see this document, which, by the way, was not addressed to him. Nobody has yet been convicted on the basis of what someone else asks him or her to do without the acts and conducts of the person in question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Without establishing the acts of the person in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do have documents stating that -- P2754. General Miletic informed the Drina Corps and the Zvornik Brigade that a unit of the 1st Krajina Corps was going into the area, but what is strange about this document, the Prosecution admitted in its opening statement on the 27th of August, 2006, page 461, when it said, speaking about the document, that it was only a matter of sending in extra troops to the fighters. The Prosecution stated that General Miletic was observing the Muslim forces, that General Miletic only reacted and received the reports. He still is a person who does not take any decisions. It is General Mladic. This is stated by the expert on the page 1618. If the report of the Zvornik Brigade addresses the issue of prisoners, these reports do not reach the Main Staff. They are sent to the Drina Corps. The military expert, Richard Butler, was quite clear when he said, on the 1st of February, 2008, on page 20971: "When we go up the chain of command, we do not address the issues that relate to the separation of people or that kind of thing." There is indeed a report which was sent to the Main Staff on the 13th of July, 1995, Exhibit PP113, but I would like to say that this was specifically sent to the intelligence services, and if by any chance General Miletic did see this report, and I do say "if by any chance he did see it" because this was not sent to him, he may have understood that an exemplary evocation was taking place in Potocari. Adequate medical care was provided, with addition to water and food which had reached the refugees, according to the report of the 12th of July, at 12.40, information forwarded over the telephone. The reports which reached the Main Staff contain so little information and are so far removed from reality that General Mladic went to see -- that General Mladic had to go on the ground to check what was happening [as interpreted]. This order by General Mladic is P927 on the record. When these officers come back to -- from the Zvornik Brigade, they have not much to say. In 2007, we have Bogdan Sladojevic who testified in 2027, page 14373. In replies to Zepa, that generals of the Main Staff on the ground, General Tolimir and General Mladic, and these are the men who are on the ground who observe how the Muslim forces are moving and their surrender. They conduct the search operation. They are observing the movements of the units of the Republika Srpska in the area, and they are the people who follow up on the transfer of the population. Those are the people on the ground, not General Mladic, not General Miletic. Not General Miletic. General Tolimir does send documents, reports, to General Miletic, but we have no evidence that Tolimir's proposals were ever implemented. We know that General Tolimir had asked UNPROFOR people not to come on the ground, and we know that they did come. We know that General Tolimir asked for chemical weapons to be used, but we have never heard anything to that effect. General Krstic also writes to General Miletic and informs him, on the 5th of July, 1995, document P3015, that Zepa had been freed. We know that on the 20th of July, 1995, Zepa had not been liberated. Why did such erroneous information reach General Miletic? We don't know. The military expert of the Prosecutor stated on the 29th of January, 2008, page 20648, and I quote: "Looking at the overall information on the subject, in many cases the VRS felt that the situation was going one way, whereas they discovered afterwards that this was not the case. Was it someone's intention or were these mistakes? We don't know." General Miletic has no other information about the situation on the ground, other than what he gets from the officers who are in the field, and none of this information tells anything about anything that might be criminal, irregular, or unusual. So where is General -- why -- how can one establish General Miletic's responsibility here? He was part of the army. The army is not a criminal body, as such. The mere fact that General Miletic belonged to this army and the Main Staff does not turn him into the person responsible for the acts committed in Srebrenica and Zepa, and the Prosecution showed no evidence that he, himself, was involved in one way or another in what happened in and around these two enclaves. The Prosecutor showed no evidence of the fact that General Miletic knew, before the Army of the Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica, that the enclave had been taken [as interpreted]. He provided no evidence that the intention of General Miletic was to drive out the Muslim population from the enclaves, to forcibly transport them, and provided no evidence that such an inference can be drawn and that that would be the sole reasonable conclusion. Therefore, I request the acquittal of General Miletic on all counts of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madame Fauveau. It's time for the break, in any case, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I suggest we have the break now, 25 minutes, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I briefly mention one matter which you might want to consider during the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that relates to timing. Now, Your Honour, I hope I'm going to be no more than the 90 minutes I'm permitted, but could I invite the Chamber to consider what it said on the 9th of November of last year at page 17837, when Your Honour, the learned Presiding Judge, stated: "We are not going to intervene or interfere as to who should go first amongst yourselves, and I think that we can safely say that you can also agree amongst yourselves to make use of any disposable, leftover time that remains, excepting that you will have an hour and a half each." Bearing in mind that my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic has not made a submission, Mr. Lazarevic has not used up all his time, am I permitted to do use in excess of 90 minutes if I need to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more? We need to finish today, basically, once we have arrived at this stage, so that next week, Monday and Tuesday, we'll have the responses. I think with your experience, Mr. Josse, you can conclude in an hour and a half. What I can offer is perhaps Mr. Haynes might entertain the idea of going first, not exceeding, say, 20 minutes that he said yesterday and that he mentioned yesterday, and then you can have the rest, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll discuss that with him, Your Honour, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's make an effort to conclude the submissions -- the Defence submissions today, once we have arrived at this stage, rather than have them continue on Monday, and then Monday and Tuesday Mr. McCloskey will finish. He said he will finish Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My difficulties will become clear as I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay, thank you. Twenty-five minutes. And the time now is 10.31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you are going first, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and you have an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Over the last two days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're starting at 11.00. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- this Trial Chamber has heard some excellent and dare I say it thought-provoking submissions which we trust will give the Chamber something to mull over. Thereafter, of particular note, you might think, was the first address from my learned friend Mr. Meek. If it is to be his swan song, then it's a performance that those of us who had the good fortune to hear it will long remember. He reminded us, rather conveniently, bearing in mind he set the ball rolling on these 98 bis submissions, of why we were here and some of the central tenets of a fair criminal justice process. Some of his assertions, in particular his quotations, most -- perhaps everyone in this room will agree with and cannot argue with. Other of his remarks were perhaps a tad more controversial. General Gvero's lawyers look forward, with genuine relish, to our opportunity to address this Chamber on the merits of the case, and we look forward to our opportunity to make submissions on his behalf as to why we contend the Prosecution have failed singularly and lamentably to prove the case against him, and we say that bearing in mind what has been said against our client, and in particular we note recently two rather strong attacks on our client by my learned friend Mr. Thayer, in particular, who, in these submissions, gave what we would characterize as a ranting type of argument more akin to a closing speech than one that was appropriate for a submission in the middle of a trial. But, Your Honour, the result of all this is that we, the general's lawyers, realise that this is not the opportunity for us to proclaim our client's innocence and it's not our opportunity to say why Mr. Thayer is wrong and why his rants should be rejected by this Trial Chamber. We do assert strongly that General Gvero is an innocent man in relation to the allegations made against him so far as both Srebrenica and Zepa are concerned, but we appreciate that our time to deal with these particular matters, our time for rhetoric, for speeches, for assertions of that sort, will come later. And as I've already said, we look forward to our opportunity to make those submissions in due course and to tell this Trial Chamber why the Prosecution case is so wrong. In the course of the submissions I make in the next 88 minutes or so, nothing should be read by this Trial Chamber as an acceptance on the part of my learned leader Mr. Krgovic or myself that the Prosecution have discharged their ultimate and heavy burden against General Gvero. Before I turn to my main submission, which is going to relate to count 8, could I say a word or two about count 7. We make no submission today in relation to count 7, but something that Mr. Bourgon said yesterday is of concern to us. At page 21265 of the proceedings, Mr. Bourgon broke down the forcible transfer count and, paraphrasing, he said that it fell into three different groups; firstly, the women and children, secondly the able-bodied men, and thirdly the members of the Muslim 28th Division. He went on to say that in his submission, count 7 applies only to the first of these groups, namely, the women, children and elderly. Now, Your Honour, let me make it clear. We wholeheartedly support that submission on behalf of General Gvero. I dare say virtually all the Defence lawyers are going to support that submission. But the reason I draw it to your attention at this stage is to ask you to consider whether now is the appropriate time to make a finding in relation to that. I'm not making a submission on count 7. Others have not made a submission on count 7. In effect, those of us who are not submitting on count 7 are deprived of an opportunity to make further submissions on what could be an important issue in the case, and our concern is that the Court will reject Mr. Bourgon's submission, which as I say we wholeheartedly support, and we will be hamstrung with that ruling for the rest of the case. And, of course, we say that our opportunity to address that important issue should come at the close of the evidence, when you consider count 7 in relation to General Gvero. Now, how that impacts on Drago Nikolic is not a matter for me to address, nor a matter for me to concern myself with, and I make no comments so far as that's concerned. I'm only concerned so far as General Gvero is concerned. But in relation to him, we submit now is not the time to make that particular ruling, in particular since we are not making any submissions upon it. Now, having said what I'm not going to talk about, namely, count 7, let me begin my address on count 8, the deportation count. And some of what I have to say has already been covered by Madame Fauveau in the submissions that she made this morning. I'm going to go into the matter in a little more detail, if I may, but forgive me if I cover ground that she has already dealt with or alluded to. The offence is contrary, as we know, to Article 5(d) of the Statute of this Tribunal, and it's a crime against humanity, and the central thrust of the submission I'm going to make, and as I say, Madame Fauveau has already made it, is that the victims, if I could use that word, in that count have to be civilians, and if they're not civilians, the count will fail. Now, the issue of crimes against humanity and what victims of crimes against humanity amount to has been extensively reviewed recently at this Tribunal by the Trial Chamber in the case of Mrksic and others, and the rather large tomb which I asked Madam Registrar to hand you at the beginning of my submissions, is that judgement, and the reason is I'm going to go through a number of paragraphs of it in some considerable detail. I've also handed a copy to my learned friend Mr. McCloskey. Those of my colleagues co-defending with me will perhaps forgive the fact that we haven't provided copies to them, but they can find this judgement on the internet which they can access at any time. Now, if Your Honours would turn to section B of this judgements which is jurisdiction under Article 5 (crimes against humanity), it deals with the chapeau requirements, it then deals with issues to deal with widespread or systematic attacks, a nexus to the attack, and I'm going to go straight to the section headed "C" directed against any civilian population, and paragraph 440, please. There, it says the attack must be directed against any civilian population. 442, the term "civilian population" must be interpreted broadly and refers to a population that is predominantly civilian in nature. "A population may qualify as civilian even if non-civilians are among it, as long as it is predominantly civilian. The presence within a population of members of armed resistance groups or former combatants who have laid down their arms does not, as such, alter its civilian nature." This jurisprudence is in line with Article 50(3) of Additional Protocol 1, and I'm paraphrasing here, going on, which states that: The presence within the civilian population of individuals who do not come within the definition of civilians does not deprive the population of its civilian character. Then it goes on, Your Honours, at paragraph 443 in a section headed "Applicability of Article 5" to non-civilian victims. I beg your pardon, I said -- I've got it right, 443. I was right. A related but distinct legal issue arises in the circumstances of the present case. While it has been clarified by the jurisprudence of the Tribunal that mere presence of non-civilians among what is a predominantly civilian population does not alter the civilian character of the population for the purposes of this chapeau requirement of Article 5, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal has not yet been called upon to pronounce the question whether the notion of crimes against humanity is intended to apply to crimes listed in Article 5, when the individual victims of such crimes are not civilian. And then the Trial Chamber deals with the question it posed to the parties. It then deals with the submissions made by the parties. I'm not going to deal with that. I'm really going to turn perhaps to the answer and the discussion. Paragraph 448, please. At the outset, the Chamber would observe that all parties appear to be in agreement that the victims of a crime against humanity must be civilians. The Defence for each of the three accused, by explicitly advancing this proposition, and Prosecution implicitly by accepting that all victims of the crime charged under Article 5 of the present indictment qualify as civilians. The issue in dispute appears to be the definition of "civilians" that should be applied. And thereafter, in the succeeding paragraphs, I can inform this Chamber that the judgement sets out the history of the matter. I'm not going to deal with that in any great detail, but we can go to paragraph 451, please, where it says: "This approach, however, was rejected by the Blaskic Appeals Chamber in 2004, when it overturned the Trial Chamber's decision. The specific status of the victims at the time of the crime may be determinative of his civilian or non-civilian status." Basing itself on Article 51 of Additional Protocol 1, the Appeals Chamber held that members of the armed forces or members of militias or a volunteer corps forming part of such armed forces cannot claim civilian status, and neither can members of organised resistance groups. Going on, if I may, to the next paragraph, it says that the jurisprudence was later followed by the Appeals Chamber in Kordic, which says that the term "civilian" needs to be defined in accordance with Article 50 perhaps I should say "(1)" of Additional Protocol 1. Moving on to 453, it says in some, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal consistently refers to Article 50 of Additional Protocol 1 when interpreting the term "civilian" in Article 5 of the Statute. It accepts that the mere presence of non-civilians among what it is predominantly a civilian population does not alter its characteristic. Again paraphrasing, Likewise it adopts the definition of "civilian" in Article 50(1) which has to be reflective of the customary international law. If I may move to paragraph 555, please, the judgement then deals with the submission that the Prosecution had made in relation to Blaskic. In the middle of that paragraph, it says: "This is precisely why the Blaskic Appeals Chamber overturned the Blaskic Trial Chamber. The criterion is not the position of the victims at the time of the crime, but their status as civilians under Article 50 of Additional Protocol 1, together with Article 4 of Geneva Convention 3," and then Article 43 of additional Protocol 1. Paragraph 457 deals with a terminological evaluation, which might be important, and basically it says that whether the conflict is international or non-international, it amounts to the same. That's how it's summarised, that paragraph, and we can then move on to 458, please, which is particularly important in the context of this case. In addition to the reasons set out above, there is yet another reason why the Chamber cannot accept the Prosecution's proposition that the definition of "civilian" under Article 5 of the Statute is broad and includes all persons who are not participating in hostilities, including combatants hors de combat. Certain crimes listed in Article 5 of the Statute can only be committed against civilians, not against combatants. For example, deportation, under Article 5(d), cannot be committed against prisoners of war. And the paragraph then, Your Honours, goes on and deals with a brief analysis of the historical origins of the crimes against humanity dealing with 6(c) of the Nuremberg Charter, goes on and deals with the requirement about an attack being widespread or systematic, and then importantly, towards the bottom of the paragraph, in that jurisprudence a preponderance criteria has been developed. The population must be preponderantly civilian, inspired by Article 50(3) of Additional Protocol 1, but this does not have the effect of abandoning the underlying principle, i.e., the crimes against humanity as opposed to war crimes, are directed against civilian victims. Paragraph 460 really deals with the importance of the Tribunal not filling the gap, if there be a gap, in the law through what's described as the telelogical interpretation, and I draw that to the Chamber's attention and what the Mrksic judgement said in that paragraph. 461 says: "In view of the above, the Chamber concludes that the term 'civilian' in Article 5 of the Statute has to be interpreted in accordance with Article 50 of Additional Protocol 1, and therefore does not include combatants or fighters hors de combat." 462 says that the Chamber is aware, and I'm paraphrasing, that the Tribunal hadn't yet decided this particular issue. The jurisprudence accepts that the attack requirement for crimes against humanity allows for the presence of non-civilians in the population. That is, the target of a widespread or a systematic attack. There is nothing to suggest that a crime listed under Article 5 of the Statute would qualify as a crime against humanity if the victims were non-civilians. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, you'll be glad to hear I'm very near the end of my review of this particular judgement, because we get to the conclusion, which is paragraph 463 and 464, so the conclusion in this judgement was: "The Chamber therefore concludes that for the purposes of Article five of this Statute, the victims of the underlying crime must be civilians. If the victims are non-civilians, the more appropriate charge is war crimes. In the view of the Chamber, this is a proper and specific requirement for the application of Article 5, which takes into account the historical origins and developments of crimes against humanity as a category distinct from war crimes. In reaching this conclusion, the Chamber does no more than to interpret Article 5 of the Statute in the context of the factual situation in which it is called upon to apply the article, which is without precedent in the Tribunal's jurisdiction. "The analysis above leads the Chamber to conclude that in order for a crime in Article 5 to constitute a crime against humanity, it is not sufficient for that crime to be part of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population. The victims of the crime must also be civilians. Accordingly, a crime listed in Article 5, despite being part of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population, does not qualify as a crime against humanity if the victims were non-civilians." Finally, paragraph 464 says there is no case law defining the required mens rea. The jurisprudence has only considered the mens rea in relation to the armed conflict, the nexus requirement and the attack. And then the remaining words are extremely important, and I'm going to analyse those in detail in a few moment's time: "As the civilian status of the victims is only a jurisdictional requirement and not an element of the crime, the Chamber believes that it is sufficient for the perpetrator to have been aware of the factual circumstances that established the status of the victim." And the Chamber might wish to look at the footnote there, which is 1722, which says: "The Chamber does not consider this to be an element of the crime that needs to be established by the Prosecutor. Under International Humanitarian Law, the civilian status of a victim is presumed, absent evidence to the contrary." And then it quotes Article -- Additional Protocol 1, Article 50(1), where it says: "In case of doubt whether a person is civilian, that person shall be considered to be a civilian." And, Your Honour, that may have some practical implications in this case, which I'm going to come to in a moment. The Defence for General Gvero accept and respectfully endorse everything stated in that judgement, except that bit at the very, very end which relates, of course, to the burden of proof. And as I say, I'll come to that in a moment. It might be worth, at this juncture, a very quick look, in terms of the framework of this legislation, for the Chamber to have in front of it both Article 50 from Additional Protocol 1, I think it is, and also Article 4, Geneva Convention 3. We've got copies of those, if that's of assistance to the Chamber, and perhaps we could hand those out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I know it's being handed up, and since you're going to have it in front of you, it's going to save me quite a lot of time. But basically the Chamber will see how Article 50(1) of Protocol 1 defines "civilian" in relevant part by exclusion from the category of combatants, and then, in conjunction with that, the Chamber can look at Article 4 of Geneva Convention 3, which defines at some length what a combatant is. As I say, I'm not going to go through that now, but that might be useful for later. What the Defence do say is that the men who crossed the Drina, or certainly to adopt the words, in fact, of the Trial Chamber in the Mrksic judgement, the preponderance of those men were undoubtedly members of an armed forces, they were combatants. Exactly which category of Article 4 they fit into is not something we suggest we need to concern ourselves with, but the legislation is there -- or the convention is there, perhaps I should say, if it's of assistance to the Trial Chamber. We contend it's certainly not our duty, that is, those defending, at this stage or indeed any stage of the case, to say which of the criterion Article 4 these men fitted into. Now, Your Honour, I said I was going to deal with this issue of the burden of proof, because it's quite seriously problematical, we suggest, what is stated in that -- in paragraph 464 and footnote 170 of 1722 of the judgement we've just been through in some detail. It appears, we would suggest, from a reading of the Mrksic judgement, that the status of the victims in question in that case was not actually in dispute, bearing in mind the concessions made by the parties, so it probably didn't matter who or in what manner the burden of proof actually lay in that case. In this case, as will become apparent when we look at the evidence in a few moments' time, it probably does matter, and the Defence emphatically reject any submission that the burden of proof on this issue shifts to the Defence. We have had an opportunity to, for example, have a cursory glance at the international edition of Archbow, and at no point does that textbook suggest that the burden ever shifts in international criminal law. Were it to do so, we would suggest, it would have to shift by an express provision in a statute. It can't shift in any other manner. In short, if it's a requirement of Article 5 of the Statute that the victims be civilians, then we contend that the Prosecution need to prove that in the normal way. We can advance some brief explanation as to why we think the Trial Chamber in Mrksic ended up with the conclusion that it did. If one looks at footnote 1722, we see the reference to International Humanitarian Law, and under International Humanitarian Law, it might well be right, in case of doubt whether a person is a civilian, that person shall be considered to be a civilian. Indeed, I have no reason to suppose it's not right. That is correct in International Humanitarian Law, but that is not to say that that is the position in international criminal law. And we submit that International Humanitarian Law needs to be read in the light of international criminal law and, in particular, the golden thread of criminal justice, which is the burden of proof, and therefore we suggest the Mrksic judgement, exemplary as it is, in that regard simply can't be right, because the reality is, if it's right, the burden on this quite important issue shifts, and if the burden shifts, then it's undermining what I've already described as a golden thread of criminal justice. Now, the importance of that is going to become clear, I hope, in the next ten minutes or so, when I briefly review the evidence on this particular topic. What is the evidence in regard for the combatant or civilian status of the men who crossed the Drina? Well, Your Honour, there are a significant number of documents in evidence, we would suggest, which indicate that this was an armed brigade, and I'm going to summarise them fairly quickly, I hope; first of all, 6D83, which doesn't need to be put into e-court and anyway shouldn't to be broadcast, but it's a document from Avdo Palic to the 1st Corps of the Armed Forces of the Sarajevo, dated the 2nd of February, 1994, giving some background to the Zepa military detachments. There's 6D73, dated the 17th of February, 1995, which deals with helicopter flights and the arming of the Zepa Brigade by the ABiH. There's 5D265, which in fact is a document dated 28th of May, 1996, but dealing with events a year earlier, and again the supply of the Zepa Brigade.
