There's evidence from Witness 49 of weapons and ammunition being delivered to Zepa by helicopter in the second half of 1994 and early 1995, at pages 9722 and 9783 of the transcript. There's the development of the arsenal of the Zepa Brigade described by the witness Savcic at 15330. There's evidence, Your Honours, of coordination between the ABiH and the 1st Zepa Light Brigade; for example, 6D73, dated the 17th of February of 1995, 5D228, dated the same day, an order from Brigadier General Hadzihasanovic to, amongst others, the 1st Zepa Brigade Command, 6D75, an instruction dated the 2nd of June, 1995; from a Captain Bektic to the Zepa Brigade giving military instructions. There's 6D77, dated the 29th of June, 1995; a report from Ramiz Becirovic to both Tuzla and to Zepa. There's the evidence of Mirko Trivic as to what he discovered, in terms of opposition, military opposition, that is, when he arrived in Zepa on the 13th of July, and what he saw thereafter. That's at page 11903.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could maybe save you some time, I will stipulate that significant numbers of those men that went across the river, perhaps even the majority, would be considered part of the army, if that will help. I think the facts are clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I smile, because that's why I wanted a right of reply. You see, the whole issue here was I, of course, have never known exactly how the Prosecution were going to respond to this submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed. Forget the reply. If there is a real need for a reply, we might consider that then, but for the time being we have no intention of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I understand, and in which case I'm going to go on, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, please, go ahead. But do take into account what Mr. McCloskey has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as best I can. There's 6D104, which is similar evidence, dated the 13th of July, 1995. I will deal with this very quickly, because I want to put it on the record. 5D275, 6D34. And then 6D107 I'll deal with in a little more detail. That's dated the 18th of July, and it's from Mr. Izetbegovic to General Delic. Number 2 in that document, it says: "Perhaps in this case we could insert a brigade or battalion of soldiers to Zepa across the forest path and thus continue the combat with more success. These men from Zepa say they could find between 500 and 1.000." Similarly, the following day, 6D36, a letter from the president of Zepa to Mr. Izetbegovic, where he says, amongst other things, the troops continue to resist. And, Your Honour, my final point in relation to this is rather ironic, bearing in mind Mr. McCloskey's helpful intervention, was a similar intervention that he made when I think it was me but it may have been another counsel was cross-examining Mr. Dzebo at 9635 of the transcript, where Mr. McCloskey says: "Just to remind counsel these issues are not in contest. We've gone over this issue and the policy of the Bosnian army, and these have been part of this Prosecution's case for a long time. So this witness is answering his question, we could go on forever with this issue, which is really not in context." If I could mention briefly Ms. Palic, because she doesn't help the Prosecution in relation to this particular issue. At 6918 of the transcript, she says: "I knew there were negotiations on the surrender of Zepa, surrender of the army, evacuation of civilians." And then at 6964, she's talking about 26th-27th of July: "Avdo of course refused to surrender at that time. He received reports that General Smith was heading to Zepa to arrange to negotiate about the fate of the troops and that's what I also heard from Visoko." So we obviously rely heavily on her use of the word "troops" in that context. We would invite the Chamber to examine in this regard the evidence of Witness 49 at page 9819, where he was commenting on an UNPROFOR document to Lieutenant General Janvier, which talks about there being 1,500 BiH troops remaining in Zepa, and Witness 49 confirmed that. General Smith's evidence was of a similar tenor at 17633 of the evidence and a few pages thereafter. General Smith's clearly of the view that he was dealing with the men in the hills, and they were military men. Now, Your Honour, one of the issues that we are not sure we need to deal with at this particular juncture, but feel we better, well, embrace it, is the position of the SJB and Territorial Defence of Zepa. Now, again, if Mr. McCloskey is going to concede that they are combatants, then I don't need to develop this particular submission. But unless he's prepared to do that, I'm going to have to go on and try and submit that they clearly did form part of the combatant body. I should say, in fact - the thought only occurs to me now - that in fact there is no evidence, as such, that anyone from the SJB or the TO actually crossed the Drina. I'm going to turn in a few moments to the one witness we've heard from. That's PW-155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think the one witness you're referring to was a police officer. I will look over the weekend, but it strikes me that a police officer is not a civilian. But I would also remind counsel that the other witness said that he was a civilian, and at this stage, at the 98 bis stage, taking that in the light most favourable to the Prosecution and the inference that this group is much like the Srebrenica column, there are going to be civilians in it, at this stage -- this is a fascinating argument, but at this stage I believe it's not appropriate, because the evidence, as it sits, is in our favour. But, again, that's so you know our position. Perhaps that will help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. When Mr. McCloskey talks about the other witness, does he mean other than 155? Was he talking about Mr. Dzebo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can get you -- it's the fellow who did actually go across the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's 155, and I'm going to turn to his evidence in some detail. We had always anticipated that the Prosecution response in this submission was likely to rely on 155, and I'm going to address that, square on, in a few moments' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in the light of what Mr. McCloskey has just said, the Chamber will be relieved to hear I'm not going to go through the competence status of the SJB and the TO. It appears that he has basically conceded that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you'll take less than the 90 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm very keen to say a few other things about one other topic, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, I wouldn't take it as conceding that. Whether a police officer is acting under his authority, a police officer is a big issue, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You'll have a right to respond, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I -- I'll perhaps deal with that in passing when I look at 155 in a few moments' time. Your Honour, could we next turn to the issue of the mens rea of this offence, because we go back, in our submission, to paragraph 464 of the Mrksic judgement, because I am trying to have my cake and eat it, because having criticised that part of the judgement where it deals with the burden of proof shifting, by the same token we do rely on what that judgement says in terms of the mens rea for this offence, because it states, and I've read it before: "It is sufficient for the perpetrator to have been aware of the factual circumstances that establish the status of the victim." This, we would suggest, indicates that the mens rea is that the perpetrator needs to know that the status of the victim is, in fact, a civilian rather than a combatant, bearing in mind everything that we've hitherto said about Article 5. In relation to the mens rea, in this case we contend that the Serbs who collectively for this purpose can be described as the perpetrators, consistently referred de facto to this group of men in its entirety as combatants. They expressed, that is, the alleged perpetrators, their willingness to afford POW status to these men and also to participate in prisoner exchange. By way of example, we'd invite the Chamber to look at 6D103, a document dated the 19th of July, where it talks at number 4 about a Serb condition, a list would be compiled of these men by the Red Cross, and they would be taken to a holding centre for processing and they would be exchanged after an agreement is reached "with our government." Number five talks about all-for-all exchange, and so on, looking at that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please always keep a distinction between Serbs, that is, Serbs from Serbia, and Serbs, Bosnian Serbs, because we would like to know exactly where, to limit or distinguish between the two ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'll do that, and I appreciate that particularly bearing in mind the facts of this count, that is important because of where these men indisputably ended up. The document I was referring to clearly refers to the Bosnian Serbs, in our submission, but the Chamber will perhaps need to read it for themselves. I mean, paragraph 5 talks about Mladic and Tolimir, immediately before the bit that I just read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness Tom Dibb, at page 16371 of the transcript, said that Mladic would like to get into a prisoner swap with ABiH troops from Zepa and BSA prisoners. And on the other side he was commenting that word from Sarajevo was to hang on, and they wanted an all-for-all exchange. 6D108, which is a Baxter document dated the 26th of July, 1995, says at one point: "Secondly, that the Bosnian fighters will lay down their weapons and accept POW status on the basis of a putative POW exchange." And it goes on about those sort of negotiations. It says later on that Torlak stated that Mladic still supported the proposals for an all-for-all POW exchange, that is, 1,500 to 2.000 men of military age from Zepa, in exchange for the BSA POWs held by the Bosnian government. And then later on it goes on about guarantees that Mladic was giving in relation to this POW exchange. Similarly, P2496, an undated document also from Lieutenant Colonel Baxter, talks about a POW exchange, and we suggest that if one looks at these documents, it's quite apparent that as far as the Bosnian Serbs were concerned, the alleged perpetrators, these men were military men, were combatants, and were not civilians, and therefore another hurdle the Prosecution need to get over at this juncture is that of the mens rea of this offence as it is defined in the Mrksic judgement. Perhaps I should also add, in relation to this argument, we'd invite the Chamber to look at the evidence of Colonel Trivic at page 11903 in this regard, his belief that these men were combatants. And at paragraph 480 of the Mrksic judgement - perhaps you could turn to that for a moment - the situation, in fact, in that case, in relation to this issue, appears quite similar. If I could go to the middle of that paragraph, it says: "Given the evidentiary difficulties, the absence of adequate evidence before this Chamber to establish a role of a few of those victims in the Croat forces in Vukovar does not establish that these victims had no such role or that the Serb forces acted in error in some cases. These matters cannot be resolved on the available evidence. It is established by the evidence, however, and the Chamber finds that the member of the Serb forces who had custody of the victims on 20th November 1991 and those who executed them that evening and night at Opcara acted in the knowledge and belief that the victims were involved in the Croatian forces at Vukovar. In their awareness of the factual circumstances, the victims were prisoners of war, not civilians. That, we say, is akin to the situation so far as count 8 is concerned and the mens rea of the alleged perpetrators of that alleged crime. Now, Your Honour, we had prepared further submissions on the history of Article 5, in effect, and of the necessity for victims of crimes against humanity to be civilians. Now, I'm going -- the Court will be grateful relieved to know I'm going to hugely summarise that by simply saying that if one looks at the juxtaposition of Article 147 in Geneva Convention number 4, and Article 4 -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you contest that, Mr. McCloskey, that in terms of Article 5 they need to be civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I hope he'll look at the Krstic law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have asked you this question so that no one gets carried with the idea that there is agreement that Article 5 is to be interpreted in that way and then in no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think everyone knows this is on appeal and this issue will be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. I am going to go through it, then, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, within the 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed. We would -- I am going to summarise it, however. Basically, we suggest that the precursor of Article 5 is Article 6(c) of the Nuremberg Charter, which defines a crime against humanity as "committed against any civilian population and includes deportation." That's taken on in Article 5(c) of the Charter of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, in similar terms. Article 2(1)(c) of (Allied) control council law in number 10 talks about the law in similar terms, and the finding of the United States Military Tribunal in the case of Alfred Krupp et al also deals with this point and was cited approvingly at paragraph 291 of the Stakic appeals judgement in this Tribunal. Going back through the history of it, in effect Geneva Convention number 4 Article -- of 1949 deals with civilian protection. It sets it out, and we submit that the avoidance of any doubt -- could I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt and for the record, Convention 4, Article 4, simply says: "Persons protected by the Geneva Convention, relative to the treatment of prisoners of war of 12th August 1949 shall not be considered as protected persons within the meaning of the present convention," which we say emphatically refers to civilians and proves our point again. Finally in this regard, a recent ICRC study on customary international law, one of 2005, states as follows at Rule 129: "Parties to an international armed conflict may not deport or forcibly transfer the civilian population of an occupied territory, in whole or in part, unless the security of the civilians involved or imperative military reasons so demand." And it says something similar in relation to non-international armed conflict. Your Honour, I said I would move on, and I'm going to, to PW-155, because that is something we need to address head-on, and we concede we need to address that head-on. As is accepted by the Defence, he is the only victim, using that word advisedly, of this crime, or alleged crime perhaps I should say, to have given evidence before this Tribunal. We suspect that the Trial Chamber might want or need, for the purpose of this submission, to scrutinize his evidence very carefully. Much of his evidence does not stand up to much examination or belief. On the essential point, it appears that he actually claimed he crossed the Drina River with one other person only. Again, if I can have a moment, I can give you the citation for that. 6836 of his evidence. Leave aside for a moment whether his evidence is truthful or not. Taken at its highest, we suggest that those two people could not possibly be said to be a representative sample of the alleged victims of count 8. If we could move into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that. One moment, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What does this amount to? Well, we, of course, submit that the victims of count 8 must be viewed as civilians. We suggest that the preponderance of the evidence overwhelmingly suggests that in fact they were combatants. We go on and submit that, in any event, it's for the Prosecution to prove the opposite, in other words, that they were civilians, and of course remembering the words of the Trial Chamber in Milutinovic and the test at the 98 bis stage of proceedings, "so that a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt" that they were civilians. We suggest that that simply hasn't happened. We've already accepted that there are arguments the Prosecution have in regard to PW-155. We've already said he appears to be the only victim called in relation to count 8, and he describes crossing the Drina with one other person only. He's silent about all the other alleged victims of this particular count. So we suggest that his evidence, in effect, is de minimis on the count and doesn't help the Prosecution at all. We also submit that his evidence, in the light of the vast amount of evidence to the contrary of what he's saying, i.e., that these men were combatants, could not allow a reasonable trier of fact to be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt at this juncture. We go on and submit this: That even if his evidence was thought at first blush to support the Prosecution case, then he's a classic example of the other limb of 98 bis, where, in the Milutinovic judgement,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY SAID
utterances.text: "However, if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction, even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution, then the motion must succeed." Now, Your Honour, it's all very well Mr. McCloskey saying there's a very low hurdle to cross, but there is a hurdle to cross, and you, as a tribunal of law rather than as a tribunal of fact, do need to make a qualitative judgement. That's what the law says, and you do need to look at this particular evidence. Of course, my submission, we only get to this point, let me emphasise again, if all my previous submissions are rejected, about the fact that he only describes crossing the Drina with one other person, there's no evidence about any of these other men at all, we totally reject Mr. McCloskey's assertion that an inference can be drawn. What inference from where? I mean, why, why, why does it follow that the column in Srebrenica is anything like these men in Zepa? There's no basis. That's pure speculation, not inference at all. The Chamber mustn't speculate, can only infer from evidence, and in fact the evidence suggests the opposite, the inference suggests the opposite. As -- but we submit, as I've already said, that the limb I've just read out from the 98 bis test as annunciated by Judge Bonomy is there for a particular, and it designs to this particular situation where the evidence is so flimsy, where the witness admittedly is so incapable of belief, combined with all the other factors in the case, that it simply can't be right to let a case go to the tribunal of fact on that basis alone. Your Honour, could I make this reference as well to remark in relation to something else that Mr. McCloskey helpfully said. The evidence is one thing, that is, the test as enunciated in Rule 98 bis, and it's accepted, as it must be, by the Defence that the hurdle the Prosecution need to get over is a very low one. But the law is different. The law isn't a case of this Chamber making a determination of law that's most favourable to the Prosecution. The law is either right or wrong. You're being invited by us to make a ruling as to law, so far as this particular count is concerned. What the Chamber can't do, we suggest, is to say, "Well, we're going to give the most favourable ruling of law to the Prosecution because that's in line with the 98 bis test." That's not right. Like any decision of law, you, the Chamber, need to come to a decision, and it's a right-or-wrong answer, or a yes-or-no answer is perhaps the best way for me to put it. It's a heavy duty to perform, but it's one that these accused can expect you to perform, and no doubt you will do so. But we do reject any suggestion that because the law might be equivocal, that favours the Prosecution. That simply isn't the position. Law is completely different to facts. Could I have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have very nearly finished on this topic. I've been reminded that I've forgotten to mention something which might be important, particularly so far as PW-155 is concerned, so excuse me if I take this slightly out of turn. But PW-155 conceded -- we'll need to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: PW-155 confirmed, 6831, that he participated in the defence of Zepa after the fall of Srebrenica, when there was intense shelling and attacks on the lines, and he also accepted that he was at a Stublik [phoen] check-point. He monitored the Drina Canyon to monitor whether Serb soldiers would enter the village and kill civilians. We would suggest that by his own admission there, that categorises him as a combatant. Excuse me for dealing with that in a slightly disjointed manner, but I've rightly been reminded that that was an important piece of evidence, and we would invite the Chamber to consider it. So, Your Honour, broadly speaking, I've got to the end of this part of my submission. I hope that the position is clear. We say that these men were clearly combatants. We've dealt with PW-155. We say the burden is on the Prosecution, it can't and doesn't shift. And we say that based on that, there simply can be no case to answer, in a true legal sense, true strict legal test, exactly what 98 bis is here for, in relation to that particular count for General Gvero and clearly result that the -- all the other accused to meet and to answer. Now, Your Honour, I was going to move on and deal with the issue that was referred to yesterday by Mr. Lazarevic at 21301 of the transcript, where he made submissions in relation to paragraph 31(1)(c) of the indictment. Again, the Chamber will be greatly relieved to know that the wind has been rather taken out of my sails by the concession of Mr. McCloskey. It's an interesting concession, because of course it suggests that counts can be split, contrary to Trial Chamber judgements in Milutinovic, Milosevic, Krajisnik, and perhaps other cases that have suggested that counts can't be split at this particular juncture of a case, because of course if the Prosecution is able to make the concession, then in reality the Prosecution is conceding that part of a count goes at this particular juncture. But on reflection, I'm not going to get into an academic discussion as to whether that's the right thing to do or whether it's possible to do. Clearly, we accept the concession, and we're glad that we don't have to answer that part of the count. There is an argument, we would contend, to say that where a count alleging murder, and in this case multiple murders is set out in this particular way, it simply can't be right to debar a Defence submission on the base that it all forms part and parcel of one count. After a resumption of the offences, these are allegations of multiple murder to be made, and if there is no case to answer in relation to particular multiple murder, then the defendant is surely entitle to do make a submission at this particular stage. However, I repeat that bearing in mind Mr. McCloskey's concession, I'm not going to develop that further, save to say that in the light of that concession, we suggest that the Chamber does need to look at all the alleged murders described in paragraph 31, the opportunistic killings, and satisfy itself, as has been suggested in another context by many of my learned friends who have gone before me, satisfy itself that there is, in fact, a case for each given accused to meet so far as those particular murders are concerned. They're specific crimes, they're different crimes, we suggest, and they shouldn't be lumped together. I've managed it in 75 minutes, Your Honour. You were right, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't expect any rewards from us, Mr. Josse, but we do appreciate your efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's all I needed to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I told Mr. Haynes before we started that I don't know of any British lawyer who requires more than an hour and a half to deal with a Rule 98 bis submission. So, Mr. Haynes, do you prefer to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would, actually, because I've informed Mr. Josse that I'd like to see Judge Kwon for once in this case, so I'm going to move to address over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. The time now according to this is 12.16. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're starting at 12.46.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- learned colleagues, I don't seem to be able to find a happy medium in this case. Either I'm leading from the front with excruciatingly long cross-examinations or I am, as on this occasion, bringing up the rear. I will make submissions on counts 2, 7 and 8, and in bringing up the rear on this occasion, having heard the excellent and well-researched submissions of all of those who have gone ahead of me, I'm bound to say I feel rather like a lonely subleton sitting on a bicycle, about to cycle across the battlefield where the tanks have already passed. I trust you know by now that I am not repetitious by nature, and I will, throughout most of these submissions, simply adopt what has been said ahead of me. I trust you will indulge me to this extent, that if I feel submissions can be improved upon, I will do so, and if I feel multiple submissions can be drawn together, I will do so. I also have a particular duty to my client, and there are specific matters I must address on his behalf. In dealing with counts 7 and 8, as it were, generically, can I make this one general observation at the outset. In my submission, the approach of the Prosecution to this indictment is inconsistent with its historical approach to those said to have been responsible for these crimes in July of 1995. To borrow a point mentioned by Mr. Bourgon, but to expand it, history relates that General Krstic faced no indictment alleging any offence at Zepa, General Zivanovic, despite the fact that he was commander of the Drina Corps until the population were evacuated from Potocari, faced no indictment at all, notwithstanding his regular lunch engagements in Eileen Gilleece and Colonel's Trivic and Andric, who were like my client, commanders in Tactical Group 1, faced no indictment at all. This, of course, is not determinative of any decision you have to make at this stage in this case, but I do submit it is an indication that the Prosecution's approach historically to the Srebrenica and Zepa offences has been zonal, consistent with the advice or the assistance they were being given by their military analyst. On this indictment, absolutely every accused has been charged with counts 7 and 8, irrespective of what position they hold in any chain of command and irrespective of their physical whereabouts at the time those offences were said to have been committed. And I submit that is ill-thought, it's illogical, it's inconsistent with the Prosecution's prior approach, and in relation to my client at this stage, it is unsupportable on the evidence. Forgive me if I deal with things in reverse, but it just seemed simpler to do so, given the way in which things have unfolded. In relation to count 8, I wholly support and identify with the submissions developed by Madame Fauveau and Mr. Josse. In our submission, on the evidence before this Court at this stage, the allegation made in count 8 is incapable of amounting to a crime against humanity. And perhaps I will say no more than that, save this: In our submission, an army has three choices. It can fight to the death, it can lay down its arms and surrender, or it can seek to withdraw, perhaps to another country. I was very much put in mind, when we heard the evidence, such as it was, about the flight of the Muslim forces across the River Drina, to a rather more glorious example of the same thing, which was on the Dunkirk beaches in 1940, when it is often forgotten that amongst the British forces were also General de Gaulle and the French troops who evacuated themselves to Britain. That wasn't a deportation, that was a defeated army retreating to safety, and that is, I submit, precisely what we have heard about to in relation to count 8. Particularly with respect to my client, can I make these few observations. The evidence is really almost beyond dispute. Vinko Pandurevic removed himself and his forces from a position some distance from Zepa on the early morning of the 15th of July. Mr. Bourgon has illustrated the point, but I will give you some references. Pages 12596 to 7 and page 12598, the evidence of Miodrag Dragutinovic. There is no evidence in this case that that force, prior to its removal, had carried out any offensive act at all. It had simply moved itself to a position and was to move further forward on the 15th at the time it was with withdrawn. The other evidence in the case I suggest amounts to this: An assault began on the surrounding villages to Zepa, which was ceased on the 19th of July. There were a succession of meetings on the 19th and 20th of July, further fighting on the 22nd of July, and a total withdrawal to the hills by the Muslim forces on the 26th of July. The evacuation of the civilian population was completed by the 26th or the 27th of July. I say, for the avoidance of doubt, we have heard not a word of evidence that would support paragraph 67 of the indictment, and therefore there was no provable act against Vinko Pandurevic, that he did anything other than move forces into place prior to an anticipated assault on Zepa. The Prosecution had it within their gift to ask Miodrag Dragutinovic whether that had happened or to ask Colonel Trivic whether that had happened. They chose not to, for their own reasons. Furthermore, the evidence of Colonel Trivic, transcript pages 11968 and 11969, on the 23rd of May, is that he was wounded on the 29th of July and that no unit of the Zvornik Brigade had returned to Zepa by then. The evidence of Dragutinovic, transcript reference is 12705 on the 15th of July -- sorry, the 15th of June, is that no unit or personnel of the Zvornik Brigade returned to the Zepa operation before the 31st of July, after they had left the area on the 15th, and even if they had, so what? Certainly Vinko Pandurevic did not return with them, and those units were not subject to his command whilst he was in Zvornik and they were under the command of General Krstic at Zepa. Accordingly, I submit that in relation to count 8, whatever your findings as to the merits of the count as a matter of principle, there is no evidence of any act by Vinko Pandurevic which might have given any effect to a joint criminal enterprise. Can I turn now to count 7. I fully endorse and align myself with Mr. Bourgon's impeccable analysis of the interaction of the two concurrent joint criminal enterprises alleged in this indictment. But with respect to Mr. Bourgon, I submit that there is probably no real argument on that point, because I submit that if you read count 7 of the indictment carefully, you will discover that, in truth, it does not aver that the march of the column was a forcible transfer. True, it does mention the movement of the column as background fact, but where the forcible transfer is particularised, and I invite you to look carefully at paragraphs 61 to 64, mention of the column is conspicuous by its absence. It is my submission that this indictment invites no such finding, that the column was forcibly transferred. It is moreover interesting to note that no such finding was made about the column in the Trial Chamber's decision in Blagojevic. Only the women and children bussed through Potocari were said to have been forcibly transferred, and you might want to glance at paragraph 616 to 618 of the Blagojevic judgement. An ancillary point, and I am conscious that I'm just adding seasoning to the mixture here - I take it you have digested the submissions made by Mr. Bourgon on this point, I'm simply adding a few little extras - of course as of the 12th of July, which is the paragraph avered in paragraph 61 of the indictment, none of the population had in fact left the enclave. Whether they were at Potocari, Jaglici, or Susnjari, they were firmly still within the enclave, and you might want to remind yourself of the geography by glancing at Mr. Ruez's map of the OPs to help you establish that fact. It's map 6 in your hard-copy binder. I shan't bother calling it into e-court. It makes an interesting comparison, the way in which the particulars of the indictment are drawn in relation to Srebrenica, with the way in which the indictment is drawn in relation to Zepa, where I submit the military men who swam the Drina are said to have been deported, how so where in count 7 the march of the 28th Division is not avered as a particular of the forcible transfer. About the bussing of the population, because I submit that that is what count 7 is about, again I adopt the submissions of Mr. Bourgon on that topic. The units present at Potocari were under the command of the Drina Corps commander, who at that time was General Zivanovic. Mr. Bourgon has dealt with control of the population leaving Potocari. I have to deal specifically with paragraph 77(a), insofar as it relates to my client. It is alleged in paragraph 77(a) that Vinko Pandurevic supported the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the population of Srebrenica and Zepa, in that he commanded and ordered forces involved in the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves from the 6th of July through the 14th of July, 1995, knowing one of the main objectives of the attack was to force the Muslim population to leave Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. I submit that that sentence is indivisible. You must find both of the averments in that particular paragraph to be proved for that to amount to an act capable of being supportive of a joint criminal enterprise. There is not one word of evidence in this case which would support a finding that Vinko Pandurevic knew one of the main objectives of the attack was to force the Muslim population to leave the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. There is not one word of evidence in this case that he had ever seen directive 7 or any document written in similar terms. Again, this was within the gift of the Prosecution. They had PW-168 here, they had Miodrag Dragutinovic here, they had Mirko Trivic here, and neither of those men, those latter men, active in Tactical Group 1, gave any evidence of their understanding of the purpose of the objective of Krivaja or Stucenica-95 [phoen] were. As to Krivaja-95, I submit that the evidence of Richard Butler can leave you in no doubt that its aims were lawful and militarily justifiable. In support of his evidence about that topic, you will recall he produced for you target maps with keys and references, and I do invite you to consider those. He also gave a very useful analogy at page 20356, lines 9 to 23, on Tuesday, the 24th of January, about the applicability of Article 239 of the Criminal Code. There is no evidence, indeed there is evidence to the contrary, that any forces commanded by Vinko Pandurevic ever fired a shell at the town. The Operation Krivaja-95 was concluded by the 9th of July of 1995, and the evidence, I submit, supports the contention that the population, during a period of inactivity, removed itself from the town, but not from the enclave, the following day. There is no evidence, I submit, that Vinko Pandurevic was aware of any wider purpose to the military operation which he conducted and prosecuted by fighting a line towards Zeleni Jadar, according to the evidence of those who fought alongside him. Accordingly, I submit that there is an insufficiency of evidence for you to conclude that he was a party to any joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the population from Potocari out of the enclave. Lastly, can I turn to count 2. I say, by way of commentary, that as a British lawyer, the concept of joint charges of conspiracy and a substantive count together is an anathema. Under British law, it is simply impossible to allege murder and conspiracy to murder. The Prosecution has to elect which one it goes with. I ask this practical, rhetorical question: What does the conspiracy count add to this indictment? How does it help you? If you cannot find, through the multiplicity of variants of culpability offered to you by Article 7(1), three variants of a joint criminal enterprise, and Article 7(3), how on earth are you going to come to the conclusion that my client entered into an agreement which, as has been eloquently laid before you, is the essence of the conspiracy, count two? In fact, and I believe this is a point that Mr. Lazarevic touched upon, and I hope I'm not being repetitive, but I'll take you to it, if I may, it's rather more than a simple conspiracy. The conspiracy is particularised in particular 36 of the indictment. Mr. Lazarevic read it out to you yesterday. I'm not going to do the same today. But in our submission, it really amounts to two separate conspiracies. First, it is said there was an agreement to execute the men of military age found to be at Potocari, and I submit, maybe boldly, that that is not a conspiracy to commit genocide. You simply could not find that a decision to kill the men at Potocari was an agreement to commit genocide. But, it is said, the initial plan was amended. Let me just check the words. Yes. This plan also encompassed the summary execution of over 6.000 other men, and this, it seems to me, is a very significant amendment to the agreement. I make this simple point: Even if you could conclude that an accused was a party to the initial agreement, you couldn't thereby land him with responsibility for an agreement subsequently amended without specific proof that he joined the amended agreement too. It's a bit like a group of people agreeing that they will go to a shop and steal. They might all agree to that, but if then a group of them go off and decide to steal from every shop in the street, without a participant being party to the further agreement, then he could not possibly be convicted of the conspiracy alleged, the wider conspiracy alleged, and that, it seems to me on the wording of count 2, is what the Prosecution seek to do here. In any event, what opportunity did Vinko Pandurevic have to be party to the wider amended agreement, said to have been amended and changed on the 12th or 13th of July? According to Miodrag Dragutinovic, on pages 12690 and 91, Vinko Pandurevic on those days was marching through the night from Viagor [phoen] towards the position to which he ultimately returned. There's not a scintilla of evidence to show that Vinko Pandurevic entered either of those agreements, less still both. In fact, if you wanted some indication of the lack of strength in that assertion by the Prosecution, I invite you to look again at the combat reports of the 15th to the 18th of July authored by him and which are Prosecution Exhibit numbers P329 to P334. Those, I submit, are the clearest evidence of a man horrified to find that prisoners had been placed in schools in the municipality of Zvornik, and not evidence of a man who had entered into an agreement to kill thousands of people. I should say formally, if I haven't, that I adopt and endorse all the submissions that have been made by Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Lazarevic, Ms. Fauveau and Mr. Josse, but in a little over 20 minutes those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes, which leaves us with this: Do you want to start today or do you wish to start on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I can say some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think we can hear what you have to say, and then I'll come to you, Madame Fauveau. Madame Fauveau needs to make some corrections to the transcript. So you can go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I can say some things today. Might as well. Maybe we'll finish in one day next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we will go for that. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, I have a few corrections, generally from names in the transcript. [In English] Page 8, line 16, the name "Milanovic" should be read as "Milovanovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the reference, please? Page 16?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Page 8, line 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 8, line 16. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Then page 15, line 17, "the orders of General Milovanovic" shall be read as "the orders of General Zivanovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Page 18, line 9, the name "Colonel Djukic" shall be read as "Colonel Djordjic." And then page 27, line 11, the Exhibit P89 shall be "P849". Then page 29, line 7, the exhibits P2750 shall be -- P2790 shall be P2750, and P976 shall be P2976. On page 30, lines 5 and 6, the sentence: "General Miletic was there neither on the 11th and the 13th," shall be read as: "General Miletic was not with General Mladic neither on the 11th and 13th." Page 34, lines 7 -- 6 and 7: "General Mladic had to go on the ground to check what was happening," shall be read: "General Mladic sent officers from Main Staff to check what was happening." And, finally, page 35, line 25: "General Miletic knew before the Army of Republika Srpska --" no, I will start again: "The Prosecutor showed no evidence of the fact that General Miletic knew, before the Army of the Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica, that the enclave had been taken," shall be read: "The Prosecutor showed no evidence of the fact that General Miletic knew, before the Army of the Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica, that the enclave was to be taken."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor. And if you could stop at 20 minutes to 2.00 instead of quarter to 2:00, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I may -- I may stop before that. I just want to clear up a few things. First of all, I want to just explain to you my intention over the next court days, and that would be I will speak briefly of the forcible transfer and deportation count, and then I will speak about the accused Pandurevic and Borovcanin, and my colleagues Mr. Thayer and Mr. Nicholls will speak about the other accused. Mr. Vanderpuye was going to speak about Popovic. However, any discussions with Popovic will now be given to Mr. Nicholls. And some of what I've heard, we will respond to. Much of what I heard were closing arguments. I think General Miletic's counsel was very detailed, as she is, and much of that, in my view, was a closing argument, and I don't think you want me to go through the kind of detail that she went through, though Mr. Thayer will be dealing with that and will provide you some detail, but we'll stay well within the time frame, and I hope that we can finish on Monday. So I will start by talking briefly about the forcible transfer and deportation charges, and the first thing I want to remind you, and I probably may not need to, but as you've heard repeatedly from the accused, they view the forcible transfer of the Srebrenica population as somehow from on the 12th and 13th mainly, that this is the crime, and that of course is -- can't be -- that's the final leg of this crime, and it's important to know that this crime is first hatched back in the spring of 1992, and we see that in the strategic objectives. And then more so in a piece of evidence that I don't know if any tribunal will see anything as clear as directive 4 in history, in that they just spell out, "We will push out the armed forces and along with the Muslim population." November 1992. The Drina Corps order that said exactly the same thing, that came out a few days later, near the end of November, was sent to all the brigades, including the Zvornik Brigade. At the time, Vinko Pandurevic was wounded in Visegrad. We won't go into Visegrad at this stage, though we may see it in cross-examination. But he comes on the middle of December. Clearly, that order stood to move out the population. And as you heard, he led -- and his forces, which were one of the best assault forces in the Drina Corps, he led the movement of the military attack and the subsequent movement of the population all the way through 1993 that led to the humanitarian disaster that brought us the Srebrenica enclave in the first place. Vinko Pandurevic is well aware of this plan, of this enterprise, and this is Eastern Bosnia. I won't go into the rest of Bosnia for you. That -- this was just Eastern Bosnia that we're talking about, but it certainly wasn't by itself. Now, for convenience and for simplicity, we've started this indictment with directive 7, March 1995, where again President Karadzic lays out: Make life impossible, make survival impossible for the residents of Srebrenica and Zepa. Here is the joint criminal operation to move those people out of Srebrenica and Zepa. If you're involved in Srebrenica or Zepa, you're part of that joint criminal enterprise to move those people out. And, of course, then the statement a little bit farther down in directive 7, another amazing statement: "Make, by restrictive permits, make the populations dependent on our goodwill, but at the same time not allow us to be condemned by the International Community." And then we see the Dutch and the Muslims' testimony about what that entailed, and I'm not going to go through that, but it was clearly a horror. It was called "convoy terror," starvation, misery. Just what was created there, I've heard that over and over again. I'm not going to -- and so have you. And then we get to Krivaja-95, which specifically, as you'll recall, cites directive 7 and says, as Mr. Butler said it did: "Reduce the enclave to its urban area," as well as divide the two enclaves. And as we have always argued, as Mr. Butler has always interpreted, reducing the enclave to its urban area draws to some 30.000 people from the outside of the enclave into a one-by-two-kilometre area and creates the nightmarish situation that we had in 1993. Now, that doesn't say attack the enclave and take it over, but it's clearly an attack on the enclave to reduce the urban area, reduce the population inside that urban area. And then it goes on to say "and create the situation for the elimination of the enclaves." Now, direct for that Krivaja-95 goes to the Zvornik Brigade. You have a copy that went to the Zvornik Brigade while Commander Pandurevic was there. Remember what 168 said, that Pandurevic didn't think the UN would let them get at -- you know, get at the enclaves. Well, he was wrong, but he certainly knew about Krivaja-95, the wording of Krivaja-95, and, from his place in history, knew precisely what the overall objective of that was. We saw this carried out. I'm not going to go over the details of that with you. I think others may, because Mr. Nicholls may talk about the attack on the civilian population, which, as in the cases before, is concentrated mostly, in our view, on the 10th and the 11th and then this pushing of the population up to Potocari and the continuing attacks and the surrounding the population, basically taking them prisoner, disarming the Dutch. This is the principal attack on the civilian population, though as you can see from reviewing Kingori's testimony, there was indiscriminate shelling of the downtown area all throughout the attack, and the one that always sticks out in my mind is when the, probably a mortar, dropped right in the middle of the crowd at the entry to the base in Srebrenica. And Vinko Pandurevic and the Drina Wolves principally led that attack, was the best force involved in that attack, along with Trivic. We had Blagojevic, Trivic, a bit of the 10th Sabotage, but the best guys in that attack were Legenda and Vinko Pandurevic, and that was attack that started pushing the population out of the rural area and into the urban area, and Vinko Pandurevic and his units were in that area on the 12th and didn't leave until the 13th of July, and so were there that entire time. And then Vinko Pandurevic, pursuant to the orders of his commanders, goes to Zepa. You'll see the attack plan. Krstic, still as chief of staff, signs in on the afternoon of the 13th, and there's a role for the Zvornik Brigade and it's laid out, and it's the attack is to start on the 14th, and the attack did start on the 14th. Now, we'll look in the record. Mr. Haynes may be correct about the evidence about what exactly we've provided the -- or proved that the Zvornik Brigade actually did. Did they move forward or not? But an attack -- you can bet that the members of the Zvornik Brigade, and you can absolutely infer, they weren't hanging around Vlasenica bars or Han Pijesak, they were at the positions they were assigned to be on the night of the 13th, they were ready to go, like a chessboard. Clearly, the chessboard started on the morning of the 14th, whether Vinko Pandurevic's units moved or whether they stayed stationary, they provided a key part of that operation, so you have absolutely a clear, strong inference at this stage that Vinko Pandurevic played -- and his unit played a significant and substantial role in the initial assault on Zepa the first day. They are there, ready to go. It's not until the next day, in the morning, that they go out to Zvornik. So I would disagree with my colleague on the points he made there. And let me just end by briefly describing to you our view of Zepa and the deportation. We believe that there's a very strong inference that with some 1.000 to 2.000 military-aged men that flee to Serbia, that there are one or more civilians in that group. At this stage, this is an inference that is absolutely appropriate for you to make. It's also appropriate for you to make it because one of those people said he was a civilian and did it. And the -- I like the name of the -- I think it was Mr. Josse who called it the "begs belief" theory, or legal theory, which is part of the law that you look at, and you now will look at testimony and determine whether or not it's so outrageous that it begs belief. Well, this guy was a victim, a man and he came in here and did his best to testify, and he told you he was not a combatant when he left and swam that river. That is enough at this stage. In addition, we believe that an army, that soldiers can be deported. I agree that prisoners of war cannot be deported -- can be deported, excuse me. You can take prisoners of war and you can ship them -- they could have shipped them to Serbia and kept them in camps. But the key element to deportation is the unlawful displacement of the group, and so you've got to see whether or not, when these people drop their weapons and jumped into the river, risking their lives, was that unlawful or not. If it is a retreat of an army, it could be lawful. But don't forget, the overall purpose of the attack -- of directive 7 was to get rid of the people, the Muslim people. That includes everybody, army, women, children, everybody. And that is still in play on August 30th or August 1st and the end of July, when this happens. And so the intention of the VRS was to get everybody out of there, army, civilians, no question about it. And then the key point to whether it's unlawful or not is whether or not the person involved has a choice. It all comes down to choice. It was one of the three choices that Mr. Haynes gave us. Do you have -- one of your choices is to surrender. Did the combat arms of the Zepa Brigade have a choice, at the end of July, to surrender? They absolutely, unequivocally did not. They knew, from the Kravica warehouse survivor who told the commander, through the word that had hit the press, through the word that, you know, these enclaves were together, what was going on in Srebrenica. They knew, reasonably so, that if they surrendered, they would die. On August 1st, there's over 7.000 Muslim men dead not far from them, murdered. They knew it. They could not -- no one in their right mind would have surrendered at that point, and you can see that from the evidence. They just refused. They chose instead to risk their lives. You've seen the Drina. It is a tough, cold, hard river. They jumped into that river. Look at the intercepts. They were putting wheelbarrows on rafts and making makeshift rafts, and they had no choice at all when they went, and that, in my view, in our view, can be deportation. Once you have the attack on the civilian population, the jurisdictional attack that we had that began when shelling started indiscriminately falling on Srebrenica town and then started dropping deliberately in the crowds, and then the people get pushed to Potocari, and then get arrested, basically, when that happens, that's the attack. Same thing with Zepa. When those people get surrounded and taken care of and basically forced on buses, that is the attack on the civilian population. And it's the resulting people have always in this institution could be -- they could be combatants or civilians. It never mattered before this recent case that came out, and perhaps the simplest way to deal with that is to offer an amendment in the alternative as a war crime. But that is an issue that will be on appeal for a long time. It's not something that I know this Trial Chamber will use in 98 bis as a sword. If that was the case, all the -- all the combatant victims at Srebrenica would have not been part of these crimes against humanity that form the foundation of this institution, and I don't think you're going to allow that to happen. In any event, I think I'm probably -- I should stop now and make way for my colleagues so that you're not keeping listening to me probably far too much, and I thank you, and we'll be back on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. So we rise now and adjourn until Monday morning at 9.00. Thank you.
